title: Designing quenching and partitioning thermal routes of medium-Mn steel intended for ultra-high-strength plates
abstract: Abstract The applicability of the quenching & partitioning (Q&P) process to medium-Mn steel intended for plates with increased cross section produced in integrated thermomechanical processing lines has been studied in this work. The modeling in JMatPro and experimental approaches using DIL805 dilatometer were used to investigate 0.17C–5Mn–0.88Si–0.76Al–0.22Mo–0.06Nb steel and optimize time–temperature parameters of the Q&P process. Standard lever rule and its novel variant were applied for a precise determination of target interrupted quenching temperatures. The Q&P variants were investigated for a wide parameters range to record the microstructural evolution tendencies: at quenching temperatures from 240 to 300 °C, for partitioning temperatures from 350 to 450 °C, and partitioning time from 90 to 1800s. The obtained samples were characterized by various phase compositions including fresh martensite, tempered martensite, and lath-type retained austenite. Obtained results showed that the steel can be air-cooled after hot working without a risk of formation of ferrite, pearlite, or bainite; however, martensitic transformation kinetics is highly dependent on the post-deformation cooling rate which is of great importance for an industrial production of this steel type. The cooling rate and quenching temperature are the most important factors determining a final phase composition of investigated medium-Mn steel intended for plates. Studies have shown that a quenching temperature of 240 °C or lower is required to stabilize retained austenite. At higher quenching temperatures, blocky martensite grains form in the microstructure. Partitioning temperature and time have a smaller impact. The most favorable phase composition was achieved by quenching at 240 °C and partitioning at 420 °C for 300 s, resulting in the highest retained austenite content (17.8 vol.%) with no fresh martensite formed during final quenching.

sections.heading: Introduction
paragraphs: A quenching and partitioning (Q&P) heat treatment was originally applied for steels containing 1.5–3.0 wt.% of Mn and 0.5–1.5 wt.% of Si/Al [ 1 ,  2 – 3 ]. This process was designed by Speer et al. [ 4 ,  5 ] for advanced high-strength steels (AHSS) to improve strength without significant deterioration of ductility. Beneficial mechanical properties of Q&P steels are related to the microstructure composed of low-C martensite and 10–15 vol.% of metastable retained austenite (RA) [ 6 ,  7 ]. The strain-induced martensitic transformation (SIMT) of RA improves the formability of steel sheet by delaying the onset of necking and enhancing work hardening rate [ 8 ,  9 – 10 ]. It was also reported that the presence of RA in the microstructure has the positive effect on toughness and ductile-to-brittle-transition temperature of Q&P steels [ 11 ]. The Q&P steels can be potentially used for lightweight automotive constructions with improved crashworthiness [ 12 ]. The Q&P heat treatment is carried out by full austenitization or intercritical annealing followed by quenching to a temperature between the martensite start (M s ) and finish (M f ) to obtain the microstructure composed of primary martensite and austenite. Afterward, the steel is reheated to a slightly higher temperature to provide carbon partitioning from the supersaturated primary martensite to remaining austenite in order to increase a fraction of RA stabilized to room temperature. The decomposition of austenite into bainite or precipitation of carbides may also occur during a partitioning step, and as a result, a reduced fraction of RA can be present in the final microstructure [ 6 ,  13 ,  14 – 15 ]. A quenching temperature is a very important parameter of Q&P steels because it determines a martensite/austenite ratio. If the quenching temperature is too high, a large fraction of austenite is produced and not all its fraction can be enough enriched in carbon during the partitioning step to remain stable during final cooling. As a result, some fraction of undesired martensite is formed [ 16 ]. This type of martensite is called “fresh martensite” or “secondary martensite” [ 1 ,  17 ]. The formation of this undesirable martensite can be caused by the formation of carbides during the partitioning step because a lower C content is available in solid solution to enrich the retained austenite [ 18 ]. The formation of secondary martensite has a negative impact on mechanical properties of steels.

The time–temperature parameters of heat treatment for Q&P steels should be designed to achieve the optimal fraction and thermal stability of RA, preventing the formation of secondary martensite in the microstructure. It is particularly challenging in case of plates, because their increased thickness leads to cooling rate gradient and, consequently, microstructure heterogeneity across the cross section.

De Knijf et al. [ 1 ] reported that the presence of secondary martensite in the microstructure of 0.25C–1.5Si–3Mn Q&P steel has a negative impact on the stability of RA and its transformation rate during deformation resulted in reduced strain hardening rate. The results of their study demonstrated that the ductility of Q&P steels can be enhanced by increasing the volume fraction of RA in the microstructure and minimizing the formation of secondary martensite. The significant difference in hardness between secondary martensite and tempered primary martensite deteriorates local formability [ 19 ] and toughness of steel [ 17 ]. Paravicini Bagliani et al. [ 20 ] reported that the carbon depletion in martensite combined with reduction of a fraction of untempered secondary martensite was crucial for improving the toughness of Q&P 0.28C–1.4Si–0.67Mn–1.49Cr–0.56Mo Q&P steel. Zhang et al. [ 21 ] reported that secondary martensite acts as crack nucleation zones due to local stress concentration. They also observed that the presence of a soft phase, such as ferrite, enhanced the strength–ductility balance of the investigated dual-phase steel. Therefore, it is very important to design parameters of a Q&P process, which minimizes the amount of secondary martensite formed in the final microstructure of steel. The Q&P heat treatment was originally designed for steel sheets [ 22 ,  23 – 24 ]. However, the presence of RA in the microstructure may also improve toughness and wear resistance, which are very important properties for thicker plate products [ 25 ]. Wang et al. [ 26 ] and Yang et al. [ 11 ] reported that RA improves the toughness of Q&P steel, but the optimized fraction and stability of this phase are required. Retained austenite is a phase showing high ductility and cracking resistance [ 27 ]. Moreover, the volume expansion resulting from the SIMT of RA contributes to blocking the propagation of microcracks [ 28 ]. On the other hand, the formation of a large amount of strain-induced martensite may induce microcracks and reduced cracking resistance of steel [ 26 ]. Therefore, it is very important to optimize the fraction and stability of RA by adjusting a carbon content, a grain size, and morphology of this phase [ 22 ,  29 ].

Designing processing routes of thicker plate products requires a special approach due to different cooling rates and thermal gradients occurring during heating and cooling, which are significantly higher than in sheet products. The thermal gradient may have a pronounced influence on the microstructure development of Q&P plate. Stewart et al. [ 25 ] reported that the differences in cooling rates between the surface and the core of water-quenched 18-mm plate may lead to the difference in temperature of core and surface reaching up to 200 °C. Therefore, assessing cooling rates at the cross section is essential to a proper design of thermal routes for Q&P steel plates. In the case of steel plates, the main challenge is to ensure high hardenability that allows for a homogeneous microstructure across the cross section. Hardenability can be improved by increasing the carbon content; however, this approach introduces several technological issues, such as reduced machinability [ 30 ]. Alternatively, chromium can be added, although it is a relatively expensive alloying element [ 31 ]. The Mn addition is an effective and cost-efficient solution, as it significantly enhances hardenability without compromising the machinability of steel. It is also important to ensure high wear resistance and surface properties of the steel plates [ 31 ,  32 ,  33 – 34 ]. Studies addressing Q&P medium-Mn sheets are available in the literature [ 13 ,  17 ,  35 ]. However, medium-Mn Q&P plates have not been systematically studied. Hence, the goal of this study is to design optimal time–temperature parameters of Q&P process of medium-Mn steel intended for plates, which allow to obtain the homogeneous martensitic–austenitic microstructure without secondary martensite. Thermal processing variants are developed for both quenching and partitioning steps.

sections.heading: Experimental procedure
paragraphs: The investigations were performed using a steel with a chemical composition listed in Table  1 . As a response to the heavy machinery and transport market demands, the investigations were intended to obtain optimized Q&P parameters for high-strength martensitic steel plates containing RA. As carbon has a deteriorating influence on machinability [ 30 ] and weldability [ 35 ,  37 ] of the steel, its concentration was limited to 0.17 wt.%. According to the literature, a manganese content respective to medium-Mn steels (3–12% [ 38 ]) is suitable for Q&P treatment as it allows to produce above 10% of RA in the martensitic matrix, which improves the steel toughness [ 39 ]. One of the important secondary objectives was to obtain high steel hardenability, which enables to apply air cooling both during a quenching step and upon final cooling from a partitioning temperature to room temperature (RT) [ 40 ]. Taking into account the increased cost of Mn addition and possible technological problems like microsegregation or PLC [ 41 ] effect, it is important to limit its concentration. However, as manganese significantly improves hardenability of steel, it was decided to add 5% of this element. The main aim of Al and Si additions is to inhibit carbides’ formation during partitioning [ 42 ]; thus, carbon may diffuse from martensitic laths to austenitic laths. The Si alloying was partially replaced by Al because the former despite stronger effect inhibiting carbides formation is harmful for galvanability of steel [ 43 ]. The role of Mo is to support high hardenability of steel and preventing hot brittleness [ 44 ]. The microaddition of Nb is added to refine a grain size of prior austenite. Table 1 Chemical composition of the investigated alloy Chemical element, wt. % C Mn Al Si Mo Nb 0.17 5.0 0.76 0.88 0.20 0.063

The ingot was cast in a PVA TePla VSG-100 vacuum furnace under argon atmosphere. The weight of the ingot prior to the removal of the head and tail, considered as scrap, was ~ 100 kg. The ingot with dimensions of 100 × 100 mm and a length of 830 mm (~ 60 kg) was subjected to hot rolling. The cast steel was austenitized at 1200 °C for 2 h prior to hot rolling. Afterward, the material was hot-rolled in the temperature range of 1200–900 °C to a thickness of ~ 22 mm using the LPS/B semi-industrial line (Łukasiewicz Research Network—Upper Silesian Institute of Technology, Gliwice, Poland).

Initial thermodynamical calculations and dilatometric tests covered determination of the critical steel’s temperatures (A c1 , A c3 , M s ) and creation of dCCT (deformation continuous cooling transformation) and dTTT (deformation temperature time transformation) diagrams. Moreover, the relation of quenching temperature–a fraction of martensite was determined for different cooling rates. Based on the initial results, a series of Q&P parameters for further dilatometric investigations was selected, which is represented in Fig.  1 . They cover the austenization at 1100 °C and simulated rolling represented by 50% deformation at 900 °C corresponding to the industrial hot rolling process. Next, the material was cooled at a cooling rate respective for air cooling (0.5 °C/s) of suitable cross section of plates with the thickness of 20 mm. The cooling rate was determined on the basis of research assuming measurements of the cooling rates in an electric furnace for sheets of 5, 12, and 22 mm thickness. The Q&P experiments were performed using different: quenching temperatures—based on analysis of dilatometric kinetics of martensitic using lever rule [ 45 ], to obtain 70–90% martensite partitioning temperatures—in the range from 350 to 450 °C as the most common range used in the literature [ 4 ,  5 ] partitioning times—from 90 to 1800s to investigate a wide range corresponding to both continuous and small-scale processes for plates and even forgings Figure 1 Heat cycle schedules applied during dilatometric investigations.
The final cooling was also performed using conditions respective for air cooling.

The thermodynamic calculations were performed using JMatPro software with general steel database v.14.1. The dilatometric tests were performed using a DIL805A/D high-resolution dilatometer. Cylindrical dilatometric samples with the diameter of 5 mm and length of 10 mm were machined from the hot-rolled material along the rolling direction. The dilatometric investigations were performed in vacuum with induction heating. Samples were cooled using helium, and a specimen temperature was measured and controlled using a S-type thermocouple welded to the central part of the sample length. The sample length changes were measured via a linear variable differential transducer (LVDT) by fused silica pushrods. The dilatometry data were analyzed according to ASTM A1033-04 [ 46 ].

After the dilatometric tests, the samples were cut in half of the length, grinded using SiC paper with grid up to 1200, and polished using diamond suspension with 3 μm and 1 μm particle sizes. The final polishing was performed using 35-nm colloidal silica to ensure a flat surface with minimal deformation. For microstructural observations using light microscopy, the samples were etched using 3% nital for ~ 4 s at room temperature. The microstructure of steel was investigated using Zeiss SUPRA 35 scanning electron microscope (SEM) operating in secondary electrons mode. The accelerating voltage of 20 kV and the working distance of 10 mm were used for the investigations. Electron backscatter diffraction (EBSD) was used to obtain more detailed quantitative information on the microstructure. The EBSD was performed at 20 kV on the sample tilted 70° and a probe current of ~ 2.5 nA with a step size of 0.1 µm. The EBSD data were processed using the OIM TSL data analysis software v. 5.3.1. For a cleaning procedure, first, a grain confidence index (CI) standardization was used employing a grain tolerance angle of 5° and a minimum grain size greater than 3 pixels [ 47 ]. Next, the neighbor orientation correlation with CI = 0.1 and a clean-up level 3 was used. The points with CI ≤ 0.1 were removed from the analysis as doubtful.

The volume fraction of RA was determined using XRD data. The measurements were taken using Co-Kα radiation in a PANalytical X’Pert Pro MPD diffractometer working at 40 kV and 30 mA. The scans in the θ–2θ range were performed with a step size of 0.01°. The Bragg–Brentano geometry was used for the diffraction studies. The identification of the phases was based on the data contained in the International Center for Diffraction Data ICDD database. The volume fraction of RA was estimated based on the average of 3 measurements using the Rietveld method.
Vickers hardness measurements were taken using a microhardness tester FB-700 at a load of 1 kgf. Ten measurements for each Q&P variant were taken, and the mean values were calculated.

sections.heading: Theoretical simulation of phase transformations
paragraphs: Designing of thermal routes of investigated steel has been started from the theoretical simulation of critical temperatures and phase transformation kinetics using the JMatPro software. The simulations of equilibrium diagram present in Fig.  2 a suggest that the A c1  and A c3  temperatures of investigated steel are 520 °C and 821 °C, respectively. The theoretical M s  and M f  temperatures are 267 °C and 143 °C, respectively (Fig.  2 b). The CCT diagram indicates that a fully martensitic microstructure can be obtained at a cooling rate ≥ 8 °C/s. The pearlitic transformation is theoretically present during cooling at the cooling rate faster than 1 °C/s. During isothermal holding above the M s  temperature, the bainitic transformation starts the fastest at 330 °C – 767 s (Fig.  2 c). The simulations of isothermal holding below M s  temperature indicated the significant acceleration of bainitic transformation, as the incubation time at 240 °C is limited to 83 s (Fig.  2 c). The acceleration of bainitic transformation is more intense with a temperature decrease. Theoretical changes in a martensite fraction with decreasing quench temperature are present in Fig.  3 . As according to the literature [ 1 ,  13 ,  39 ], the optimal RA fraction should be about 15–20%, the proper range of quenching temperature should be between 150 and 200 °C. Figure 2 The results of thermodynamic calculations showing:  a  a microstructure evolution as a function of temperature,  b  simulated CCT diagram,  c  simulated TTT diagram. Figure 3 Changes in a martensite fraction depending on the quenching temperature.

sections.heading: Dilatometric investigations
paragraphs: The theoretical results were experimentally verified using dilatometry (Fig.  4 ). The initial dilatometric investigations indicated that the experimental A c1  and A c3  temperatures are 688 °C and 934 °C, respectively. A visible increase in sample’s length taking place directly after A c1  temperature is related to the Curie point [ 47 ]. For M s  temperature, the investigations showed that in case of the hot-deformed samples, it depends on a cooling rate: For the fast cooled material (60 °C/s) the M s  temperature is 291 °C, and for the slowly cooled one (0.05 °C/s), it is 259 °C, which means over 60 °C difference. It may be related to the process of static recovery and recrystallization occurring for slowly cooled samples (at a cooling rate of 0.05 °C the cooling time takes about 6 h). In both cases, all fraction of austenite was transformed to martensite as M f  temperature was recorded, which is not sensitive to cooling rate. However, for the Q&P process of hot-deformed steel this observation is extremely important because the quenching temperature of steel determines its final mechanical properties. The absence of any transformation other than martensitic during cooling at a rate of 0.05 °C indicates a lack of agreement between the experimental and theoretical results (Fig.  2 b). Figure 4 Dilatometric results concerning: phase transformations during  a  heating and  b  cooling of the samples at two different cooling rates.

The experimentally determined dCCT diagram in Fig.  5  indicates that regardless of applied cooling rate in the range from 60 to 0.05 °C/s the only martensitic transformation was registered. It confirms very high hardenability of steel provided by Mn and Mo additions. The dCCT diagrams again show the changes in M s  temperature depending on a cooling rate of the steel. The hardness results show its decrease with a decrease in a cooling rate of the samples. In the cooling rate range from 60 to 1 °C/s it is about 485 HV1 and next it drops to 445 HV1 at a cooling rate of 0.05 °C/s. This change is related to self-tempering of formed martensite during very slow cooling. Figure 5 Dilatometric dCCT diagram ( a ) of investigated alloy and resulting hardness values ( b ); the experimental cooling curves in air for plates with thicknesses of 5, 12, and 20 mm were plotted on the graph.

As the steel is intended for air-cooled ultra-high-strength plates, it was necessary to determine experimental air-cooling rates for such products. For this reason, tests were carried out using three plate thicknesses: 5, 12, and 20 mm. The plate samples were placed in an electric furnace until the desired temperature was reached and then removed and left to cool in the air. Temperature changes were examined by a S-type thermocouple located in a hole in the core of each plate. The cooling rate decreases with an increase in plate’s thickness. For the 20 mm plate thickness, the cooling rate is faster than 0.5 °C/s; therefore, such cooling rate was selected for further investigations.

For a detailed description of the phase transformation kinetics in the steel, the dTTT diagram (Fig.  6 ) was created taking into consideration phase transformations taking place both above and below the M s  temperature of the alloy at a cooling rate of 0.5 °C/s. Above M s  the bainitic region is very narrow as it covers only about 40 °C. The shortest incubation time was recorded for the isothermal temperature of 350 °C (2 s). At higher temperatures, the incubation time is much longer (250 s at 380 °C). Below M s  temperature, the bainitic transformation kinetics is much faster. The incubation time is reduced to below 1.5 s, and also the transformation finish occurs faster. Results reported in work [ 45 ] show that the formation of prior martensite before isothermal holding step accelerates the bainite formation kinetics in steel containing 3 wt.% of Mn. It is due to an increase in a number of preferential nucleation sites for bainite formation. Figure 6 Dilatometric dTTT diagram ( a ) of investigated alloy with isothermal holding above and below M s  temperature and resulting hardness values ( b ).

These results indicate that the holding time after initial quenching in the Q&P process should be as short as possible not to form unwanted bainite. The hardness of steel after isothermal holding above M s  temperature is consistent and equal to about 485 HV1, which is similar to the quenched steel hardness. In case of holdings below M s  temperature the hardness is lower, which is related to tempering of martensite formed during the initial cooling and isothermal holding.

As the quenching temperature is one of the most important parameters of the Q&P process, it has to be precisely selected. The investigations indicated that the M s  temperature depends on a cooling rate after hot deformation; therefore, the proper quenching temperature has to be determined for the exact cooling rate. Figure  7  shows an example cooling curve with the recorded martensitic transformation. The martensite formation is related to the sample expansion because of the body centered cubic (BCC) lattice parameter, which is bigger than for face centered cubic (FCC) [ 47 ]. If the thermal expansion coefficient was the same for both FCC and BCC lattices, the determination of changes in a martensite fraction would be easy to determine. However, both lattices have different thermal expansion coefficients, which imply more complex procedure. The most commonly used method for such determination is a level rule [ 45 ]. In Fig.  7 a modified method is proposed, in which initially a linear function tangent to the 100% austenite and 100% martensite functions has to be determined. Next by modifying variables of one of the lines, a line with a given % slope change is created and plotted on the graph. The cross section of this line with the dilatometric curve is the temperature for a given martensite %. The summary graph of this method for different cooling rates is present in Fig.  8 a. It clearly shows that with an increase of cooling rate the martensitic transformation occurs at lower temperatures. For 80% of formed martensite the difference between the cooling rates of 10 and 0.5 °C/s is almost 30 °C. Figure 7 The method for determining a fraction of formed martensite depending on a quenching temperature:  a  linear function tangents to the dilatometric curves of fully austenitic and martensitic microstructures and  b  linear functions respective to different martensite fractions. Figure 8 Summary results of the determination of the martensite fraction depending on a quenching temperature for ( a ) different cooling rates and the magnified curve at a cooling rate of 0.5 °C/s ( b ).

The changes in a martensite fraction with a decrease in temperature for the selected cooling rate of 0.5 °C/s are present in Fig.  8 b. It indicates that the interesting range of quenching temperature for the investigated steel is between 240 and 280 °C.

Figure  9  indicates that this method differs significantly from the experimental ones. The same tendency is observed in case of the changes in martensite determined using the JMatPro software. The results indicate that the currently available thermodynamical models are not accurate at least for new medium-Mn steels, and the martensite transformation kinetics has to be determined experimentally.

sections.heading: Optimization of Q&P parameters
paragraphs: Basing on the initial investigations, a range of Q&P parameters was established. The steel is designed for plates; therefore, to accurately simulate the production process dilatometric samples were initially heated up to 1100 °C; next, they were cooled to 900 °C and deformed by 50% to simulate finishing hot rolling conditions. Next, the cooling at a cooling rate of 0.5 °C was applied (simulation of air cooling) to the quenching temperature in the range from 240 to 300 °C to produce different fractions of martensite. Since the bainitic transformation below M s  temperature occurs fast (Fig.  6 ), the sample was held only for 1 s and next it was reheated to the partitioning temperature range from 350 to 450 °C within 90–1800s. Such a range of parameters allows to identify the optimal Q&P thermal route. The final cooling was performed also at a cooling rate of 0.5 °C to simulate air-cooling conditions. Figure  10 a presents the full Q&P thermal route for different quenching (QT) temperatures and partitioning at 400 °C (PT) for 300 s (Pt). The Q&P curves were compared to the fully quenched sample. The reheating and partitioning step is identified on the graph as a curve of increasing RCL as a function of temperature. It is related to an increasing size of the sample both by an increase of its temperature (linear thermal expansion) and bainitic transformation [ 49 ]. The final relative change in length (RCL) values are at a similar level for all Q&P samples and the quenched sample. Figure  10 b shows the dilatometric curve up to the quenching temperature. It indicates that depending on a quenching temperature, the martensitic transformation achieves a different level, which is represented by an increase in a RCL value. The Q240 sample expanded the most, which means that it should contain the highest fraction of martensite. Figure  10 c presents the partitioning step as a function of time. The changes in RCL are very small, which indicates that the possible processes of bainite (RCL increase [ 49 ]) or carbide (RCL drop [ 50 ]) formation are irrelevant. Final cooling of the samples is present in Fig.  10 d. An intense martensitic transformation started at 302 °C is visible in the sample quenched initially to 300 °C. The highest fraction of fresh martensite was formed in the specimen quenched to the highest temperature of 300 °C. It is also reflected in the highest hardness (448 HV1) of the sample quenched at 300 °C (Table  2 ). It means that too high fraction of austenite remained in the microstructure after the initial quenching, which could not be sufficiently stabilized by C diffusion during partitioning. Therefore, during the final quenching it transformed into martensite instead of being retained to room temperature. With a decrease of the quenching temperature, the martensite transformation signal during final cooling is weaker and starts at a lower temperature (244 °C for the sample quenched initially to 260 °C). For the Q240 sample, there was no martensite transformation recorded during final cooling, which implies that the remaining austenite should be retained to room temperature. Therefore, among all the quenching temperatures, the Q240 sample exhibited the lowest hardness (409 HV1). Figures  11  and  12  present the dilatometric data for different partitioning temperatures for quenching at 240 °C and 260 °C. Based on earlier results, they are the most promising quenching temperatures. In both cases, the signal from the isothermal holding (partitioning) step (Figs.  11 a and  12 a) is stable. Therefore, it may be assumed that no significant fraction of bainite was produced. In case of final cooling, all Q260 samples (Fig.  11 b), regardless of the partitioning temperature, exhibit the martensitic transformation start at a similar level of about 250 °C. The M s  temperature decreases slightly with an increase in partitioning temperature. A similar trend is observed in the hardness measurement results (Table  2 ). It may be also seen that an increase of the partitioning temperature leads to less intense martensitic transformation during cooling, which suggests that a higher fraction of RA is stabilized to room temperature. In case of Q240, the similar tendency for M s  temperature was observed; however, for samples partitioned at 400–450 °C, no martensitic transformation was recorded, indicating full stabilization of remaining austenite fraction. Therefore, Q240 and P420 were selected for the experiments concerning different partitioning times (Fig.  13 ). The M s  temperature was recorded only for the sample partitioned within 90 s (228 °C). The partitioning time 90 s was to short to sufficient enrichment of austenite in carbon diffuses from martensite. For longer partitioning times, the cooling curves do not contain any disturbances, suggesting the presence of martensitic transformation. Figure 11 Dilatometric results for a quenching temperature of 260 °C and different partitioning temperatures for 300 s:  a  a partitioning step,  b  final cooling to room temperature. Figure 12 Dilatometric results for a quenching temperature of 240 °C and different partitioning temperatures for 300 s:  a  a partitioning step,  b  final cooling to room temperature. Figure 13 Dilatometric results for a quenching temperature of 240 °C and different partitioning times at 420 °C.

The dilatometric results obtained for different Q&P variants are summarized in Table  2 . The fraction of RA estimated using the XRD method for different Q&P variants is presented in Figs.  14 ,  15 , and  16 . It was observed that as the quenching temperature increased, the fraction of RA in the final microstructure decreased (Fig.  14 ). The large fraction of austenite formed during first quenching was not sufficiently enriched in carbon during a partitioning step. Therefore, it transformed into fresh martensite instead of remain stable in the final microstructure. The most promising partitioning temperature range in terms of stabilization of RA is between 400 and 450 °C (Fig.  15 a, b). At the partitioning temperature below 400 °C, the RA fraction was reduced due to formation of undesirable fresh martensite observed both for the samples quenched at 240 °C (Fig.  12 b) and 260 °C (Fig.  11 b). The most promising partitioning time in terms of RA stabilization is 300 s (Fig.  16 ). The highest fraction of RA ~ 17.8 vol. % and no fresh martensite was achieved in the sample quenched at 240 °C and next partitioned at 420 °C for 300 s. Prolonging the annealing time beyond 300 s resulted in a relatively high fraction of retained austenite (~ 13–15 vol. %), accompanied by a noticeable decrease in hardness. Specifically, the sample partitioned for 1800s exhibited a hardness approximately 16 HV1 lower than that of the sample annealed for 300 s, which is attributed to the extended tempering of the primary martensite fraction, as also reported in [ 51 ,  52 ]. These findings indicate that increasing the partitioning time results in reduced mechanical properties. Figure 14 Volume fraction of RA in the samples quenched at different temperatures and next partitioned at 400 °C for 300 s. Figure 15 Volume fraction of RA in the samples quenched at 260 °C ( a ) and 240 °C ( b ) and next partitioned at different temperatures for 300 s. Figure 16 Volume fraction of RA in the samples quenched at 240 °C and next partitioned at 420 °C for different times.

sections.heading: Microstructural characterization
paragraphs: All physically simulated Q&P variants resulted in positive highly refined and lath-like microstructures (Figs.  17  and  18 ). For the sample quenched to 240 °C (Fig.  17 a) and next partitioned at 400 °C for 300 s, the microstructure is composed of tempered martensite (“lower” darker phase) and retained austenite (bright laths located above the tempered martensite). It confirms the dilatometric results that no fresh martensite was formed during final cooling. With an increase of quenching temperature (Fig.  17 c, d) the fresh martensite regions were identified in the microstructure, which can be recognized by their localization above the tempered martensite, as is the case with RA, but characterized by a darker, non-homogeneous “rough” surface. These differences in SEM imaging result from the previous etching of the steel in nital, which dissolves fast the tempered martensite, then the fresh martensite, and has less effect on RA. The microstructural state of samples after quenching at different temperatures is highly consistent with the dilatometric results (Fig.  10 ). Figure 17 SEM microstructures after the Q&P treatment with quenching at:  a  240 °C,  b  260 °C,  c  280 °C, and  d  300 °C; RA—retained austenite, MT—tempered martensite, MF—fresh martensite. Figure 18 SEM microstructures after quenching at 240 °C and partitioning at 420 °C for:  a  90 s and  b  1800s; RA—retained austenite, MT—tempered martensite, MF—fresh martensite.

Figure  18  shows the SEM images of samples quenched at 240 °C and partitioned at 420 °C for 90 s and 1800s. Some fraction of fresh martensite can be identified in the microstructure of the sample partitioned for 90 s (Fig.  18 a), where the dilatometric results revealed also the martensitic transformation (Fig.  13 ) during final cooling. The sample partitioned for 1800s is composed of fine tempered martensite and RA (Fig.  18 b).

Further microstructural details were revealed using the EBSD method. Figure  19 a and d shows the image quality maps of specimens quenched at 240 °C and partitioned at 420 °C for 90 s and 1800s. The dark regions of low pattern quality represent fresh martensite formed during final quenching to room temperature because the fresh martensite had higher dislocation density than tempered martensite formed during initial quenching [ 1 ]. It was observed that as the partitioning time increased, the width of the RA laths (marked in red) increased (Fig.  19 b, e). The magnification of the areas marked in red in the image quality maps presented in Fig.  19 c and f revealed that the thin laths of RA are located between laths of tempered martensite. Larger RA laths transformed into fresh martensite during final cooling due to their lower thermal stability (Fig.  19 c). It was reported in the literature [ 53 ,  54 ] that the stability of RA increases as the lath/grain size decreases. Figure 19 EBSD maps of specimens quenched at 240 °C and partitioned at 420 °C for 90 s and 1800s: image quality maps ( a ,  d ), phase distribution maps, RA marked in red ( b ,  e ), image quality maps correlated with phase maps ( c ,  f ); MF—fresh martensite.

sections.heading: Discussion
paragraphs: Results presented in the current manuscript are focused on designing and optimizing the heat treatment conditions for the Q&P process. It is an essential step toward the practical application of the designed thermal treatment routes. The Q&P parameters were selected to reflect industrial conditions as much as possible. The final stage of the research will involve validating the developed Q&P-based technology under industrial or semi-industrial conditions.

Until now, the Q&P heat treatment has primarily been applied to first generation of AHSS sheet steels containing about 1.5–3 wt.% of Mn. Although these steels exhibit favorable mechanical performance, they also present technological limitations that must be addressed for successful processing [ 25 ]. A key challenge is to ensure sufficient hardenability to produce a homogeneous martensitic–austenitic microstructure without the presence of other structural constituents such as pearlite or bainite, which reduce the ductility and impact toughness of steel. Zhou et al. [ 55 ] reported that applying thermal route consisting of quenching, partitioning, and tempering steps to a 20-mm-thick 0.3C–1.5Mn–1.5Ni–Nb plate resulted in microstructural inhomogeneity. Martensite formed in the surface and subsurface regions of plate, while the core exhibited a mixed microstructure composed of martensite and bainite. The addition of Mn effectively enhances hardenability without compromising the machinability of the steel, which is often a concern in steels containing less than 3 wt.% Mn, where hardenability is typically achieved through increased carbon content (0.3–0.6 wt.%) [ 56 ].

According to the above results, the most crucial parameter of the Q&P process is the first quenching temperature. It determines an initial fraction of austenite, which is available for further stabilization (Fig.  20 ). If the selected quenching temperature results in retaining too high fraction of austenite, the following partitioning will not be able to stabilize it, regardless of the applied partitioning temperature and time (Fig.  21 ), as the total content of carbon in the steel as well as its diffusion rate at the partitioning temperature does not allow the M s  austenite temperature to drop below room temperature. Moreover, an excessive increase in temperature and partitioning time is not only uneconomical due to increased energy consumption, but may also lead to the precipitation of carbides from austenite [ 57 ,  58 ], which deteriorates mechanical properties of steel, especially impact toughness. The above research indicated that at least for the analyzed medium manganese steel, the methods of calculating changes in the martensite fraction depending on a quenching temperature based on thermodynamic calculations differ significantly from the experimental results. Works [ 38 ,  59 ] indicate that these differences may be explained by the inaccuracy of currently available models in the used software [ 19 ,  21 ]. Diffusion kinetics is not included at this stage of the model development and needs to be addressed in future model improvements. The differences may be also influenced by the non-equilibrium conditions of experiments in comparison with the equilibrium nature of the calculations. Figure 20 Differences in a martensite fraction at a given quenching temperature during cooling after deformation and subsequent cooling at a different rate (0.5 °C/s and 10 °C/s). Figure 21 Influence of the Q&P parameters on stabilization of RA;  a  quenching temperature;  b  partitioning time;  c  partitioning temperature.

The performed measurements and calculations indicated a significant impact of a cooling rate after hot deformation on the M s  temperature and martensite formation kinetics (Fig.  20 ). The differences are the highest near the M s  temperature and become smaller with the progress of martensitic transformation as the M f  temperature is similar regardless of the applied cooling rate (Fig.  5 a). This phenomenon is especially important for the integrated production lines, where the heat treatment is performed directly after hot working.

Our experiments indicated that for 0.17C–5Mn–0.88Si–0.76Al–0.22Mo–0.06Nb steel the optimal quenching temperature of 240 °C should provide 15–20% of austenite. At a higher quenching temperature it was not possible to stabilize completely austenite (Fig.  21 a) despite applying different partitioning temperatures and times (Fig.  21 b, c). The partitioning time also seems to have the impact on the RA stability. In the sample partitioned at 420 °C for only 90 s, the martensitic transformation during final cooling was noted and the M s  temperature was about 228 °C. After increasing partitioning time to 300 s, the martensitic transformation was not recorded by dilatometry and not observed on SEM images. A partitioning temperature has less impact on the general RA stability because increasing the temperature by 100 °C resulted in only 13 °C change in M s  temperature. It should be mentioned that excessive lowering or increasing the partitioning temperature may result in the formation of bainite or even pearlite [ 57 ] in the microstructure and excessive tempering of martensite. In Q&P-type steels, the amounts of Si and Al significantly influence the formation of fresh martensite and bainite in the microstructure. Kaar et al. [ 13 ] reported that the addition of Si to Q&P-type steel containing 4.5 wt.% Mn effectively delays bainite formation during the partitioning step. They also observed that the addition of Al to medium-Mn steels can reduce the formation of undesired fresh martensite. In our study, the contents of Si and Al were optimized to 0.88 wt.% and 0.76 wt.%, respectively, to obtain the most favorable microstructural characteristic and resulting mechanical properties.

It should be noted that the M s  temperature measured by dilatometry during final cooling does not concern all the austenite remaining in the sample, but only its blocky grains (Fig.  22 ). In case of Q&P processing, the martensitic laths divide the original austenite grain into smaller areas during quenching. If the amount of formed martensite is sufficient, all the remaining austenite as thin laths can be quickly enriched in carbon. If the growth of martensitic laths is stopped too early, areas of blocky austenite remain in the microstructure, whose stabilization is very difficult. This type of austenite undergoes martensitic transformation during cooling, while interlamellar austenite remains stable [ 49 ,  58 ]. For this reason, despite reducing the quenching temperature by only 20 °C, the M s  temperature decreased by more than 244 °C upon quenching to different temperatures (Fig.  21 a), as the blocky austenite grains were transformed into lath-like martensite–austenite constituents. Figure  23  shows the fresh martensite (dark regions) of high dislocation density, which was formed as a result of martensitic transformation of blocky-type austenite during final cooling. It was confirmed by the presence of Kurdjumov–Sachs (yellow) of (111)γ//(011)α and [101]γ//[111]α and Nishiyama–Wassermann (green) of (111)γ//(011)α and [112]γ//[011]α orientation relationships between martensite and retained austenite [ 60 ,  61 ]. Figure 22 Retained austenite and fresh martensite in the Q&P sample quenched at 300 °C and partitioned at 400 °C for 300 s;  1  blocky grains of austenite transformed during cooling to fresh martensite,  2  lath-like RA grains between laths of martensite retained to room temperature. Figure 23 EBSD phase map displaying the Kurdjumov–Sachs (yellow) and Nishiyama–Wassermann (green) orientation relationships between the fresh martensite and retained austenite in the sample quenched at 240 °C and partitioned at 420 °C for 90 s. RA marked in red.

sections.heading: Conclusions
paragraphs: This investigations addressed designing optimal time–temperature parameters of integrated Q&P process in 0.17C–5Mn–0.88Si–0.76Al–0.22Mo–0.06Nb steel intended for ultra-high-strength plates via thermodynamic calculations and physical simulations using dilatometry. The obtained microstructures were quantitative and qualitative assessed using XRD, SEM, and EBSD methods. The main conclusions extracted were: The designed Q&P thermal routes can be easily implemented in the industry because simple air cooling can be applied to produce high-strength plates with a microstructure composed of martensite and retained austenite without harmful secondary martensite. It is possible due to high hardenability of investigated steel provided by the increased 5% Mn content. The cooling rate applied after hot deformation is a key parameter of the Q&P process. The cooling rate affects significantly the M s  temperature and martensite formation kinetics. The differences are the highest near the M s  temperature and become smaller with the progress of martensitic transformation. The M f  temperature is similar regardless of the applied cooling rate. The crucial parameter of the Q&P process is the first quenching temperature. Too high quenching temperature results in a high fraction of austenite in the microstructure, which cannot be sufficiently enriched in C, regardless of the applied partitioning temperature, and as a result, the M s  temperature of austenite cannot be reduced below room temperature, which induces the formation of fresh martensite during final cooling. The partitioning temperature affects the phase composition of investigated steel to a lesser extent. The M s  temperature decreases slightly with an increase in partitioning temperature. The difference in M s  temperatures between the lowest partitioning temperature of 350 °C and the highest partitioning temperature of 450 °C was 13 °C. The most beneficial phase composition was obtained for the specimen quenched at 240 °C and subsequently partitioned at 420 °C for 300 s. The highest fraction of retained austenite (17.8 vol.%) was obtained, and no fresh martensite was formed during final quenching. The limited partitioning time prevents possible tempering of the initial martensite. The cooling rate of 0.5 °C/s characteristic to air cooling can be applied to plates with a thickness of 20 mm to produce homogeneous martensitic–austenitic microstructures with a hardness of about 470HV1 in the entire cross section of the plate.
